**The Weight of a Name**

The first time I heard the word *exile*, it was whispered in a half-empty café in Prague. I was twenty-three, sitting across from a man who had once been a poet in his homeland but now lived in the shadows of a language he barely spoke. His name was Viktor, but he told me it was a lie—*a name given by the state, not by the blood*. He traced the rim of his coffee cup with a trembling finger, the way people do when they’re about to say something they can’t unsay.

“Names are the first things they take,” he said. “Then they take your face. Then they take the sound of your voice when you speak your own language.”

I didn’t understand then what he meant. I thought exile was a place—some distant country where people went when they were kicked out. But exile, I learned later, is a kind of slow drowning. It’s the way your reflection in a mirror starts to look like someone else’s. It’s the way your hands forget how to write in your mother tongue. It’s the way you begin to dream in the language of the people who now call you *foreigner*, *guest*, *the one who doesn’t belong*.

---

I was born in a city that didn’t exist on any map until my parents decided to make it real. My father, a geologist, had found a valley between two mountain ranges where the soil was rich and the air was thin with something like hope. He named it *Eldoria*—a word he made up, a name that sounded like a fairy tale but was, in truth, just a place with no history, no ghosts, no weight. The first settlers called it *The New Beginning*, but we just called it home.

I grew up in a house with too many books and not enough walls. My mother was a librarian who believed in the power of stories to save souls. She read to me before I could read myself, her voice a lullaby of far-off lands and forgotten kings. She told me that names were more than labels—they were promises. *You are named after your grandfather’s courage*, she’d say. *Your middle name is the sound of the river where your great-aunt drowned.* Names were the threads that tied us to the past, even when the past was just a story.

But names, like everything else, can be stolen.

---

The first time I felt the weight of my own name was when I was twelve. I had just moved to a new school, and the other kids kept mispronouncing it. *Ell-ee-uh*, they’d say, like they were trying to make it sound like an insult. *Ell-ee-uh*, as if it were a joke. I started changing it in my head—*Ellie*, *Lee*, *Lina*—anything to make it fit. But my mother found out.

“Names are not for changing,” she said, her voice sharp as broken glass. “They are not for hiding behind.”

I didn’t tell her about the boys who called me *Foreigner* in the hallway. I didn’t tell her about the way my stomach twisted every time someone laughed at my name. I just nodded and went back to pretending it didn’t matter.

But it did.

---

Years later, I found myself in a country where the language curled around my tongue like a snake. I had come to study, to escape the suffocating smallness of Eldoria, to see if I could become something more than the daughter of a geologist and a librarian. But the words wouldn’t stay. They slipped through my fingers like sand. *I am sorry*, I tried to say. *I love you*. The syllables came out wrong, clumsy, foreign.

A professor once told me, “You will never fully belong here. And you will never fully belong back there.” I wanted to argue with him. I wanted to scream that names were just names, that language was just a tool, that belonging was something you chose. But I knew, deep down, that he was right.

---

Viktor died in a fire. The news came in a text from a cousin I hadn’t spoken to in years. *He was in his apartment. The fire department said it was an accident.* Accident. That was the word they used. As if a man who had spent his life being told he didn’t belong could just *accidentally* burn to death.

I went to the funeral. The coffin was open, and his face was unrecognizable—swollen, blackened, as if his soul had finally escaped the prison of his body. His daughter, a girl of sixteen, stood beside me, her eyes red and hollow. She had taken his name when she was born, but she had never really known him. She had only known the man who had been told to forget his own.

“He used to say,” she whispered, “that names are the last things we keep. That even when they take everything else, they can’t take the name you give yourself.”

I didn’t know what to say. So I said nothing.

---

Now I live in a city that doesn’t exist on any map. Not officially, anyway. It’s a place where the streets are named after poets and revolutionaries, where the air smells of old books and rain. I have a name here—*Lina*, *Lee*, *Ellie*—but it doesn’t matter. I am still the girl who was born in a place that wasn’t on any map, who spoke a language that wasn’t quite hers, who carried the weight of a name that was both a gift and a curse.

Sometimes, when I’m walking down the street, I hear my mother’s voice in my head: *Names are promises.* And I wonder if I’ve kept mine.

---

The truth is, I don’t know if I ever will. But I know this: names are not just words. They are the first and last things we give ourselves. They are the way we say, *I exist.* And even if the world tries to take them away, even if it tries to erase us, we can still whisper them in the dark.

We can still be named.
